english: We would be treated fairly if we were allowed to defend the cause of truth before educated judges—or, since that is denied us for now, if at least we were not battered by the uproar of the ignorant.

And since we suffer the loss of raising a trophy for the churches’ salvation—a trophy that discerning judges would have awarded our just cause with remarkable support—at least the crowd’s approval should have no further power to insult us. Of the two groups I have mentioned, one would then help us and the other do us no harm, if the first possessed authority or the second a sense of shame. But affairs are deeply confused, and fools are very numerous. The church is being robbed of reason’s steering gear so that popular doctrine can sail on with its horn held high.

Thus, when the wise are allowed little while the worthless are allowed whatever they please, the judgment of virtue has been expelled from the churches by the decree of rioters. What counts against us among the common people is our refusal to swell the ranks of error. I mean the crowd that weighs the worth of an opinion by its success and judges it truer the more people it sees approving it.

Cicero says against Epicurus that there is clear evidence his teachings lack subtlety: people of every sort everywhere declare that they like them (Cicero, Tusculan Disputations 4.7). These people, perversely as in everything else, treat that as evidence of wisdom.
For lustful souls positively delight in slandering every holy person who has ever lived anywhere, so that the examples of distinguished deeds will not rebuke them.

They positively delight in—and are deeply attached to—pleading nature’s weakness, saying that the flesh is subject to sins from birth, and placing the achievement of reform outside the human will. They call the crimes of deliberate conduct the functions of bodily parts. They say that the catholic faith consists in confessing a free will, but one through which a person is compelled to do evil and cannot will the good.

They call the teaching of those who assert that a just God created humanity free to act well empty and heretical human talk: the teaching that each person has the power to turn away from evil and shine through the pursuit of virtue. For this would drive the sting of anxiety and fear into those who attribute their shameful acts to the necessities of the flesh.

Finally, in churches that enjoy great honor and large congregations, they preach that sin has such power that, before the limbs are formed and before the soul begins or arrives, it flies over the seed as it is deposited, invades the mother’s hidden chamber, and makes the unborn guilty. Guilt, older than birth itself, waits for the substance to exist. Then this law of sin, dwelling in the limbs, compels the captive human being to serve crimes—a person who, even in shameful conduct, deserves pity more than punishment. For what we call the faults of an evil will is called an inherited affliction in the church by men, women, and eminent bishops (allusion to Romans 7:23).

added_allusions.reason: Law of sin in the limbs taking a person captive.

english: These, then, are the whores of the Manichaeans, pandering to people’s ears with their utterly filthy doctrines.
This nettle has stirred up our enemies of both sexes. Formerly its sting, produced by the vice of evil habit, was nevertheless treated with the ointments, so to speak, of wholesome exhortation.

But now it has begun to be offered as medicine, and pleasure has gained the support of authority. With almost the whole world’s consent, shamelessness runs riot: the queen of minds, ruling through the bodily organs, the conqueror of decency, the undefeated captor of every soul. The more honorable our defense of truth, the harder it has therefore become. For the few who heal through speech have little power against reckless crowds hostile to their own remedies. What then? Should we sound the retreat at the sight of them, avenge the insults we have suffered by keeping silent, and laugh at others’ shipwrecks from the safe harbor of our conscience? But first, the goodwill we owe the human race opposes such hatred. So do our hope and faith in God. Besides repeatedly restoring the seemingly hopeless wreckage of the times, God has rewarded with eternal recompense the steadfastness he wished us to exercise until death, even when no result followed in the present.

Rejoicing, then, in this comfort of faith, let us press on with the work we have begun and fulfill our promise to argue the case. We do not doubt that this itself is a very great part of our reward: we stand in the citadel of a doctrine which, though attacked by the envy of so many and the error of still more, has risen so far above uncertain fortunes that it enjoys an invincible reputation, holding victory in its possession.

For if, as the preceding discussion has shown and the following discussion will show, everything belonging to reason, learning, justice, devotion, and the testimony of sacred Scripture supports the doctrine we defend, all our enemies’ efforts achieve nothing except to prove them utterly shameless before every learned person, utterly defiant before the holy, and utterly irreverent toward God.

The advocates of inherited sin have nothing to set against the force of the reasoning that crushes them. Their other writings bear witness to this, and so do the little books we are answering. Addressed to a military man who, as he himself can acknowledge, is occupied more with other business than with literature, they beg for the help of unrestrained power against us. In their own support they keep recommending the decisions of little crowds, whether of country people or theatergoers, although no history records the deliberation by which those decisions were issued.

Yet we certainly cannot deny what I have said: filthy crowds greatly enjoy blaming nature for the offenses of the will and defending moral wantonness by slandering human seed. The result is that no one tries to correct what he expects something else within him to be committing.

But the feeble protection offered by blind opinion increases sins; it does not diminish them. This itch of miserable people who willingly make themselves sick will carry no weight against reason itself. Yet they claim that certain scriptural passages, especially the words of the apostle Paul, establish natural sin. I postponed explaining those passages until the second book, and now it is time to fulfill that promise. First, to equip the reader better, I will briefly distinguish what has been done from what remains. We have shown that nothing can be proved from holy Scripture which justice cannot uphold. If God’s law contains justice in its perfect form, then its adversary, injustice, can gain no strength through that law. Consequently, authority cannot defend what reason disproves. Next we proved that God is known to us by his virtues. We must therefore confess his justice just as we confess his almighty power. If his justice is allowed to collapse, his whole majesty will begin to totter. God is just in such a way that, if he were proved unjust, he would be proved not to be God. We concluded that we worship God in the Trinity as perfectly just, and it became irrefutably clear that he cannot charge infants with someone else’s sin.
Just as we discussed the definition of justice, we also discussed the nature of sin. Sin proved to be nothing other than an evil will that was free to refrain from what it wrongly desired.
Thus the clearest evidence taught us conclusively that there is no sin in newborn children, since the exercise of the will cannot be found in them.

Clear reasoning also showed that those who say sins are natural deny free will. Indeed, the Carthaginian denied it, not in his own words—lest they carry too little weight—but with a testimony from the Gospel (John 8:36), as though that gave his denial greater authority. By explaining this testimony, we restored it to the Gospel’s dignity. We also freed the apostle Paul’s testimony from the slanderer’s snares and, with the prophet as witness, showed that our God, the potter of good vessels, is the creator of everyone (Romans 9:21; Isaiah 45:8–13).

added_allusions.reason: God as potter and human beings as vessels.
The preceding book 1.138 explicitly identifies this prophetic passage in the argument recalled here.
Recalls the earlier dispute about the Son setting people free and whether that denies free will.

english: These are the principal points established in the first book. Any one of them alone is amply sufficient for the victory of truth. Although the further work is more than necessary, it remains for us to discuss the Teacher of the Gentiles’ statement that sin entered the world through one man (Romans 5:12). We will use the definitions already given whenever necessary and prove that reason has said nothing false. It is an act of injustice to charge some people’s births with other people’s deliberate deeds. Through testimonies from the law, in this book or the next, we will also show that this very injustice displeases God and is forbidden by him, although no one should have doubted it. These points necessarily establish both that we are entirely right to maintain that no one is born with sin and that God cannot judge newborn children guilty. Free will is therefore as intact as each person’s nature is innocent before the exercise of that person’s own will.

The Manichaeans, however, rebel against both devotion and reason. They suppose that sin exists before the time of willing, which the nature of things does not allow; that the one they argue to be unjust is God; and that holy Scripture deserves slander, since they claim its written records establish a crime on the part of the deity. But none of these three things can be demonstrated by reason: neither sin without will, nor injustice in God, nor perversity in the law. Only they themselves are shown to be foolish, shameless, and impious.

Above all, then, let the discerning reader hold firmly to this: all sacred Scripture contains only what catholics understand to honor God, as the light of its many statements makes clear. If a difficult expression raises a question, it is certain that the passage’s author did not intend anything unjust. It must be understood in accordance with what clear reason and the brilliance of other, unambiguous passages have disclosed. Let us now set down the words of our opponent. In that part of his argument where he had brought his God to the point of being a potter of sinners—the argument we opposed in the preceding book—he briefly said that sin entered the world through one man, without dwelling on the passage’s explanation (Romans 5:12). After many words against the excerpts he says were sent to him, however, he reached a passage of mine which he set before himself as though to attack it. Yet he offered nothing that answered the attack made on him. Instead, he took refuge in the apostle’s statement that sin entered the world through one man, and tried to explain the passage’s whole sequence in accordance with his own doctrine. For this reason I have passed over other matters and hurried to this part. Since I promised to resolve this question in the second book, I wanted both to keep that promise and to show what his argument actually was. Otherwise I might be thought dishonest for suppressing his explanation and supplying the one we acknowledge as catholic (see Against Julian, Unfinished Work 1.113).

added_allusions.reason: Explicit statement that sin entered the world through one man.

english: In my first work, then, I examined his statement: ‘For just as sin, whether infants derive it from this source or that, is the devil’s work, so a human being, whether born from this source or that, is God’s work’ (Augustine, Marriage and Desire 1.1). I quote it here as it stands in my own work, from which this man had stolen a very large portion.

There I replied: ‘With due respect to your teaching authority, you are evading the issue. But understand that the truth has taken away your freedom to wander. Look: we too agree that sin is the work of an evil will, or the devil’s work. But through what is this sin found in an infant? Through the will? Yet there has been no will in the infant. Through the body’s form? But God gave that. Through the soul’s arrival? But the soul, newly created by God, owes nothing to bodily seed. Through marriage? But marriage belongs to the parents’ activity, and you previously said that they did not sin in this act. If that concession was insincere, as your subsequent argument indicates, marriage itself must be cursed for causing the evil. Yet marriage has no substance of its own: its name designates people’s activity. The parents, then, whose union caused sin, rightly deserve condemnation. There can therefore no longer be any doubt that married people are consigned to eternal punishment, since their activity enabled the devil to gain dominion over human beings. If you concede this, you lose everything you previously seemed to maintain: namely, your statement that a human being is God’s work. For the offspring’s origin lies in the union of bodies. Therefore, if evil comes into human beings through their origin, and the devil’s right over human beings comes through evil, it necessarily follows that the devil is the maker of human beings, since the origin of those born comes from him’ (quoted in Augustine, Marriage and Desire 2.44–49). After this I repeated his words: ‘For just as sin, whether derived from this source or that, is the devil’s work, so a human being, whether born from this source or that, is God’s work.’ At once I challenged him as follows: ‘When I think of that frightened statement of yours that marriage is not evil, I cannot consider these other remarks without laughing. If you believe that human beings are made by God and that married people are innocent, see how impossible it is to maintain that original sin is derived from them. Certainly the one born does not sin, the one who fathered the child does not sin, and the one who created the child does not sin. Through what cracks, amid so many defenses of innocence, do you imagine sin has entered?’

He therefore set this continuous passage from my earlier work before himself in his second book, although with alterations (Augustine, Marriage and Desire 2.44–49). For he passed over, by design I suppose, my mention of the body’s formation and the soul’s arrival. Reason, the authority of sacred law, and the catholic church all establish that a new soul is created by God in each person.

He then assembled the rest, although varying some expressions. Against these objections of mine he devised nothing that could strike back at me. Confessing through his lack of an argument that my conclusion was true, he says that the apostle must answer all these points for him—the apostle who declares that sin entered this world through one man (Romans 5:12). At this point, what educated person could think him sound in the head? He did not understand that he should either pass over objections against which he could find nothing, or think up some answer to them and attach the apostle’s words in support of it.

added_allusions.reason: Explicit statement that sin entered the world through one man.

english: I asked, then, in strict logical sequence, as all learning will acknowledge with me, through what sin—the work of an evil will, which is also called the devil’s work—could be found in an infant. Through the will? Even our present opponent admits that no such will has existed in the infant. Through marriage? No one doubts that marriage belongs to the parents’ activity, and he had previously stated that they did not sin in this union (Augustine, Marriage and Desire 2.46). If our debater regretted this concession, as the course of his work indicated, he should admit that the parents are guilty, since their union prepares a kingdom for the devil over God’s image. I added, by the necessary steps of argument, that original sin makes the devil the creator of bodies. For if evil comes into human beings through their origin, and the devil’s right over human beings comes through evil, the devil is the maker of human beings, since the origin of those born comes from him. Realizing that these arguments would imprison the advocates of inherited sin in the Manichaeans’ cave, I turned the key to give the captives a way out. I warned him that, if he truly believed human beings were made by God and sincerely confessed married people innocent, he should understand that original sin cannot be derived from them. ‘Certainly,’ I said, ‘the one born does not sin, the one who fathered the child does not sin, and the one who created the child does not sin. Through what cracks, amid so many defenses of innocence, do you imagine sin has entered?’ (Augustine, Marriage and Desire 2.47). What, I ask, could have been framed more reverently, truthfully, clearly, briefly, and firmly than my drawing a fourth proposition—the decisive conclusion—from the three premises my opponent had conceded? Sometimes one or two premises necessarily establish a third. By what rule, then, should I be forbidden to infer the fourth proposition that follows from three admitted premises? And this is only in the second argument. In the first, five or more points are conceded to me, after which a valid and undefeated conclusion follows.

Let us now turn to him. You had granted me that sin is an act of the will. I could immediately have said, as a consequence: ‘But infants have no will that sins; therefore infants have no sin.’ Yet to press you with more witnesses I asked, step by step, through what this sin could be found in an infant. Could it perhaps be through the will? Then, with your acquiescence, I adopted the premise that the infant had had no consciousness of willing. I added the question whether the infant had acquired the outlines of its limbs through the first fault. But you had conceded that God shapes them and that they are therefore good. Third, I asked whether you thought guilt was brought in through the soul’s arrival. Yet it was established that this soul was new and owed nothing to the seed. Next I asked whether, since nothing in these things remained for you to accuse, you called marriage—that is, the union of bodies—the devil’s work. But, again with your agreement, I showed that this belongs to the parents’ activity. Once everything mentioned above had been acquitted, your doctrine of transmission enslaved to the devil the married people who had caused the sin. After all this I drove home the consequence approaching you: you believe the devil is the creator of bodies, since you assigned to him the work of sexual union without which bodies could not originate. This argument showed the disease oppressing you. The second showed both how pitiable you are with such views and how invincible the catholics remain, supported even by your fear. You conceded that God makes human beings, that married people are innocent, and that infants perform no acts on their own. From these three premises it was irrefutably inferred that, when the one born does not sin, the one who fathered the child does not sin, and the one who created the child does not sin, no crack remains through which sin can be shown to have entered. If you dislike the conclusion, then deny your concession. Say that either the one who fathered the child sinned, or the one who created the child, or the child who was born. Of these alternatives, one is insane, another Manichaean, and the third goes beyond the Manichaeans: insane if you say infants commit offenses; Manichaean if you accuse married people; beyond the Manichaeans if you consider God the author of sin. But if all these things are so far from the truth that you still fear to confess them openly, with what shamelessness, most senseless of men, do you persist in denying the conclusion we have drawn?

The case here concerns four persons: God the maker; the two parents, from whom the material is supplied to the maker; and the infant who is born. You say sin dwells in this company. I ask who commits it. God? You say no. The father? Again you say no. The mother? The same answer. The infant? No. And you still do not think it has been proved that something none of these four commits cannot exist among these four?

What, then, will you try to persuade us of by rereading Scripture or naming people who agree with you, when you still cannot define your own view? What good does it do you to prove that Adam sinned, something I do not deny at all? Adam died so many centuries ago. Our question is through what sin is found in an infant—the sin by which God’s image is transferred to the devil’s ownership.

If it comes through the parents’ union, openly condemn the marriage your argument condemns, and spare us the work of proving you a Manichaean. But if you do not dare say this, and, defiant of reason, bow to those having intercourse, you produce unheard-of monstrosities of argument. You say that lust is diabolical and, although located in the feelings of those coupling, provides the parents’ pleasure but the newborn children’s guilt. You certainly expose your own madness and shamefulness. But please do not presume so far as to think we are not free to defend newborn children’s innocence while honoring God, when you are permitted—and pleased—to accuse God while clearing the lustful people’s own bodies of what you call lust’s guilt.

For when you declare that the prince of darkness planted sexual desire in humanity, and that it is the devil’s shrub producing the human race from itself as its own fruit, you clearly betray yourself: you call the devil, rather than God, the creator of human beings. By this utterly impious doctrine both the business of marriage—that is, genital union—and all flesh are condemned.

But after this blasphemy you add that, while you profess the pleasure of married people who beget children to be diabolical, and the movement of the genitals diabolical, nevertheless neither the moving organs themselves nor the married people experiencing pleasure are guilty. Instead, for all these things you accuse new human beings: the deity’s fresh handiwork in newborn children. You abandon none of the Manichaeans’ impiety, but display such monstrous madness of a deranged mind that it would more properly be judged a condition to nurse than to cut away—except that the ruin of many people, your obstinacy, and your proliferation of writings testify to your deliberate will and zeal in this matter.
Read the fourth book of my work on this subject too. You will understand how much, under the guise of accusation, you flatter the devil whom you call your father, and lust, your mother.

But let us now examine the words of the apostle, whom you said answers everything I set out above. You write: ‘The apostle answers all these points for him. He accuses neither the infant’s will, which does not yet exist in the infant as a personal will capable of sin; nor marriage, insofar as it is marriage, which has not only its institution but also its blessing from God; nor the parents, insofar as they are parents, lawfully and legitimately joined to one another to produce children. Instead he says: “Through one man sin entered the world, and death through sin; and so it passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Romans 5:12). If these people received this with catholic ears and minds, they would not have hearts rebelling against Christ’s faith and grace. Nor would they vainly try to twist these completely clear and evident apostolic words into their own peculiar, heretical meaning. They claim that this was said because Adam sinned first, and thereafter anyone who wished to sin found in him an example of sinning. Thus, they say, sin passed from that one man into all human beings, not by generation but by imitation of that one man. Yet surely, if the apostle had meant imitation here, he would have said that sin entered this world and passed through all human beings through the devil, rather than through one man. For Scripture says of the devil: “Those who belong to his party imitate him” (Wisdom 2:24; Latin numbering 2:25). But he said “through one man,” from whom the generation of human beings certainly began, precisely to teach that original sin passed through all people by generation’ (Augustine, Marriage and Desire 2.45).
translator_notes: The Latin text of Romans 5:12 says in quo, rendered here as “in whom”; the interpretation of these words is part of the dispute. Wisdom’s wording and verse division follow the Latin quotation; modern Wisdom 2:24 corresponds to Latin 2:24–25.

english: Any educated reader of our works understands that you abuse your supporters’ ignorance and hide behind ambiguous words. The remaining crowd, of whom the prophet says to God, ‘You have regarded human beings as the fish of the sea’ (Habakkuk 1:14), are deceived as they follow one another’s lead. Ignorant of the distinctions that would save them, they think everything they see joined in words can also be joined in reality. Only a very learned and attentive person can judge what follows, what conflicts, and what the invincible and venerable law of argument requires one to infer from given concessions.

That is the chief reason why, grieving over the churches’ ruin, we appeal to examination by men distinguished for their wisdom: to reveal not merely what is said, but what is said consistently. If the dispute were heard before such a council, you would certainly not be allowed to assert what you had denied or deny what you had affirmed. But in your book, which no discipline of shame restrains, you boldly heap together what catholics say and what Manichaeans say. You are content with this one impression: that people say you have answered. You think it pointless even to consider what weight or consistency your argument possesses.

In fact, you grant what I asked without hesitation. Seeing what follows from these concessions, you acknowledge that you are powerless against the case we have built. You say the apostle Paul opposes everything we have said, yet introduce him as conceding the same points you had conceded. For you say: ‘The apostle does not accuse the infant’s will, which does not yet exist in the infant as a personal will capable of sin’ (Augustine, Marriage and Desire 2.45). Once this is granted, it is already proved that there cannot be any sin in the infant. For sin, even according to your own definition, has no other nature than the will to commit what justice forbids and from which one is free to abstain.

If, then, the apostle does not accuse the infant of a personal will, understanding that such a will could not yet have existed, he certainly declares that no sign of guilt appears in the infant. This is especially true when the judge is justice, which imputes no sin except one from which abstention is possible. But, not content to grant this alone, you add: ‘Nor does the apostle accuse marriage, insofar as it is marriage, which has not only its institution but also its blessing from God’ (Augustine, Marriage and Desire 2.45). This by itself could equally suffice to overthrow natural sin. For if the apostle knows, as he does know, that marriage is not to be accused, and if the pleasurable union of the sexes, instituted and blessed by God, belongs to marriage as its means and instrument of union, then no possession by the devil can sprout from marriage. Nor is its fruit guilty, especially before that justice which imputes no sin except one from which abstention is possible.

Let us consider the third point, too, so that your generosity may be seen in your readiness to agree. ‘Nor does the apostle accuse the parents, insofar as they are parents, lawfully and legitimately joined to one another to produce children’ (Augustine, Marriage and Desire 2.45). Weigh what you have said: the apostle does not accuse the parents insofar as they are parents. He therefore declares that, insofar as they are parents, they cannot bear fruit for the devil, and that nothing coming from them insofar as they are parents belongs to the devil. Children, however, belong to parents precisely insofar as they are parents. Children are therefore proved neither guilty, nor under the devil’s kingdom, nor liable to accusation by the devil. To make our point clear by repetition: the union of the sexes contributes to offspring insofar as the married people become parents. If, however, they choose to behave more wantonly with one another, or stray into unlawful adulterous intercourse, that cannot concern their children, who are born from the power of seed, not from the obscenity of vices.
Therefore what passes from those who beget to those born is not their shameful conduct but their seed. God instituted the power of seed and, as you are compelled to confess, blessed it.

Children, then, are not guilty even when their parents sin in begetting them. For parents are connected to their children only insofar as they are parents; correspondingly, children are connected to their parents only insofar as they are children. It is established that offspring share in their progenitors’ nature, not their fault. If you declare that the apostle confirms what reason demonstrates, then we rightly defend, under his instruction, the position that parents’ sins cannot belong to their children. The apostle, radiant with the Holy Spirit; we, instructed by reason’s light; and you, crushed by the weight of the truth you attack, all jointly and truly confess that parents, insofar as they are parents, are not guilty. They are connected to their children only insofar as they are parents. Consequently, children insofar as they are children—that is, before performing any act through their own will—cannot be guilty.

Let the ingenious minds of Manichaean reasoning now go and attempt everything they can. Let them endure the toil of thought for as long as they please. Reverently, not arrogantly, I promise that this structure can never be shaken.

With what effrontery, then, do you add: ‘But through one man sin entered the world, and death through sin; and so it passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned’ (Romans 5:12)? You interpret this to mean that the apostle says sin was transmitted from that man to his descendants by generation (Augustine, Marriage and Desire 2.45). Above, you had conceded that the Teacher of the Gentiles does not accuse marriage, which God blessed; that no will to sin exists in the newborn child; and that parents, insofar as they are parents, are lawfully and legitimately united to produce children. Immediately you add, as though you had said the earlier things in your sleep, that guilt is transmitted to descendants by generation. If they beget only insofar as they are parents, and insofar as they are parents are lawfully and legitimately united, and this union is not disapproved by the apostle because God not only instituted but also blessed it, with what mouth, by what rule, with what effrontery do you maintain that this generation is the cause of guilt, a root of crimes, and the devil’s slave?

So it does not deserve accusation by the apostle, yet is possessed by the devil! It is instituted by God, yet is a fountain of crimes! Finally, it is blessed by God, as you confess, yet accused by you of being the devil’s shrub!

All literary learning testifies that you have achieved nothing against me. The conflict between your statements shows how you struggle against the apostle and rage against God. But now that we have shown that things separated by their very nature cannot be joined, let us question the apostle too. Otherwise the barbarity proved to exist in your statements might be thought to exist in his understanding.

I hear Paul declaring: ‘Through one man sin entered the world, and death through sin; and so it passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned’ (Romans 5:12). You maintain that this was said with reference to generation, not to an example of sin. You call us heretics for referring it to examples, and imagine that this argument helps you: ‘Surely,’ you say, ‘if the apostle had meant imitation, he would have said that sin entered through the devil and passed through all human beings, rather than “through one man.” For Scripture says of the devil: “Those who belong to his party imitate him” (Wisdom 2:24; Latin numbering 2:25). But he said “through one man,” from whom the generation of human beings certainly began, precisely to teach that original sin passed through all people by generation’ (Augustine, Marriage and Desire 2.45). But I see that the apostle said nothing intended to slander human generation, condemn natural innocence, or accuse God’s work of crime.

In fact, you tried to infer by argument what the words themselves had not indicated. You add that, if he had been speaking about imitation, he ought to have mentioned the devil; but because he meant generation, he preferred to say ‘a human being’ rather than ‘a demon.’ I therefore ask what gave you occasion for this opinion. What? Do you deny that people sin by imitating human beings? Although so plain a matter needs no scriptural testimony, listen to David: ‘Do not compete with evildoers or envy those who practice injustice’ (Psalm 37:1; LXX/Vulgate 36:1); ‘Do not envy the one who prospers in his way’ (Psalm 37:7; LXX/Vulgate 36:7). Moreover, all the Old Testament Scriptures warn Israel not to imitate the practices of an impious nation (compare Leviticus 18:3; Deuteronomy 18:9). What necessity, then, required the apostle, if he meant imitation, to name the devil rather than a human being, when he knew that people sin by imitating both human beings and the devil? Either prove that no one can sin by imitating human beings and that this is found nowhere in the law, and then maintain that room has been made for your conjecture; or else, since it is evident that nothing has strengthened sins more than the imitation of vices, acknowledge that you inferred with great ignorance that the apostle would certainly have spoken of the devil if he had meant imitation.

added_allusions.reason: The explicit summary of warnings not to imitate foreign nations recalls this prohibition.
Explicit summary of the law forbidding imitation of the nations’ practices.

english: It is clear, then, that imitation of evil human beings is not merely a consistent expression but a necessary one. For the moment, it is evident that this argument of yours lies defeated. You add that Scripture says of the devil, ‘Those who belong to his party imitate him’ (Wisdom 2:24; Latin numbering 2:25). I too agree that the author of that book, whoever he is, said this wisely. But the statement that some sin by imitating the devil does not help you unless you show that people cannot sin by imitating human beings.

Both expressions are customary. Sometimes a person envies because he has imitated the devil; sometimes, by copying a human being, he is stained with envy or the filth of shameful conduct. The word ‘imitation’ can therefore apply to either person, whether one is speaking of a human being or of the devil. Your insistence that Adam could not have been indicated in connection with imitation is ridiculously foolish.

The discussion hurries toward what remains, but we must press this point further, dividing it as briefly as possible to help the reader both understand and remember it. In almost every area we find homonyms, which we call words with more than one meaning.

To keep our discussion on the matter at hand: generation properly concerns the sexes, while imitation always concerns minds. This disposition of a mind that imitates what it freely chooses either incriminates a person or advances him, according to the different circumstances. Thus, in good conduct, a person is said to imitate God, angels, and apostles. God: ‘Be perfect, as your Father is perfect’ (Matthew 5:48). He also declares that those who have obtained abundant grace reign in life through one—a grace which benefits those who imitate virtue. No question about the ‘one’ therefore remains. The added statement that those who receive abundant grace reign in life also resolves the first statement: no one is driven to death unless he has embraced the sinner’s example.

The life in which the holy will reign is shown to be eternal. Therefore the death that follows voluntary wickedness should also be understood as eternal. ‘Therefore, as through one man’s offense it came upon all human beings to condemnation, so through one man’s righteousness it came upon all human beings to justification of life. For just as through one man’s disobedience many were made sinners, so through one man’s obedience many will be made righteous’ (Romans 5:18–19). Every difficulty is resolved. It is shameless to stir up a false accusation about universality; it is utterly foolish to hunt for a knot in a smooth rush. The apostle declares that not all but many learned sins through the first man’s disobedience, and that many, not all, obtained righteousness through the other’s obedience. Human origin is not under discussion here. Conduct is displayed in opposing pursuits. Disobedience and obedience show the activity of deliberate conduct, not of generation. Surely, if the apostle thought as you do, where could he more fittingly have declared that all go to condemnation by birth but few to life by believing, than here, where the argument’s conclusion was to be completed? He ought to have said: ‘Just as through one man’s disobedience all were made sinners’—or rather, not ‘through disobedience,’ but ‘Just as through the first man’s generation all were born sinners, so through one man’s obedience many will be made righteous.’

Had he put it that way, the statement would have been shown as impious as it was foolish. The comparison itself would be utterly stupid, because the persons were presented on different terms and unlike things were compared: nature and will. On the evil side he would place the necessity of seed, but on the good side only freedom of effort—or rather, no freedom any longer, since the power to choose good and avoid evil would not be available if guilt were natural. The apostle, then, the church’s wise and learned teacher, says that sin arose and passed on through disobedience, and that righteousness multiplies (compare Romans 5:19).

english: Consequently, he destroys the theory of natural sin and teaches that the causes of substance and of will are different. Lest this understanding be attributed more to our ingenuity than to apostolic teaching, let us hear what he added to this passage: ‘But the law came in,’ he says, ‘so that the offense might abound. But where sin abounded, grace abounded beyond it, so that, just as sin reigned into death, grace might reign through righteousness into eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord’ (Romans 5:20–21). Maintain, then, how your sin—the sin of inherited transmission—began to abound after the law, and what increase it received after Moses’ ministry.

You certainly contend that in these passages the apostle discussed natural sin. Earlier, he said it existed until the law, so that we would understand it ceased after the law. Now, however, he says of the same sin that it began to grow and abound after the law. We have shown that both statements fit the catholic understanding we follow. But with what shamelessness are they claimed for your doctrine, so that one and the same sin is said earlier to have ceased when the law was given, and now to have grown? How, then, did natural sin abound after the law? Did the genitals begin to move more fiercely, so that increased and novel movements seem to have added power to your sin? Or was a law given to newborn children, admonishing those begotten from sexual desire—which you call diabolical and the root and fruit of sin—to amend what they had been made, and correct the activity they had undergone when their parents begot them? Were they finally to compel what had happened not to have happened, and by refusing to hear this incur the crime of disobedience? No fool, much less the law God gave, could charge them with that (compare Romans 5:13; Romans 5:20).

english: What, then, was added after the law to natural sin, which is shown in the law not to have been prohibited or condemned, nor even lightly censured or faintly disclosed?

Certainly even you are not so senseless as to say that sin transmitted by descent became greater after circumcision. How, then, did it abound after the law when it is neither accused nor revealed in the law? But see how well this agrees with the sound understanding that places sin solely in the wrongdoer’s will. The apostle says sin existed until the law, so that after the law it should be understood as transgression (Romans 5:13): it crosses commands that have been promulgated. In this way sin abounded when the law came in, because transgression added odium to its guilt. The act of an evil will, which before the law was sin, after the law also began to be transgression. Yet God did not give the law with the purpose of making mortals worse through its enactment. For the law is neither sin nor the cause of sin, but ‘the commandment is holy, just, and good’ (Romans 7:12). Wrongdoers’ perversity, however, wounded itself with the blade that should have healed it, and opposed God’s purpose, so that it found danger where it should have found healing. The apostle says that the outcome of events injured the apparent purpose of God’s decision to give the law. Human amendment did not result as the lawgiver intended; rather, the opposite occurred in very many people. He says sinners’ efforts went so far that the law seemed given for no other reason than to make the wicked more wicked and add transgression to sin.

In this sense, then, the offense is rightly said to have abounded: each person’s will committed it both before and after the law, but before the law the will was sinful, while after the law it was also transgressive. Something grows and abounds when it gains increase within its own kind, just as after Moses the additional weight of transgression was added to the sin of free will. For it belonged to the same kind, though at a different time: an evil will which sinned both before and after the law, not through irresistible compulsion, but through blameworthy effort. Since this is so, nothing in the apostle’s words can fit your position. The coming of the law is not shown to have made inherited sin more abundant or greater. Nor can something plainly unrelated to newborn children’s will rightly be said to abound through sins of will. Therefore what the law could neither prohibit nor punish did not abound after the law. ‘But where sin abounded, grace abounded beyond it, so that, just as sin reigned into death, grace might reign through righteousness into eternal life’ (Romans 5:20–21).

As he proceeds, the apostle explains himself more clearly. He teaches that, when human salvation was being lost, God, moved by the abundance of his compassion, brought a medicine more effective than usual to a desperate situation. Those whom he had not corrected by commands he would bind to himself by benefits, requiring devotion for the future while not imputing past deeds. People should then strive to preserve the righteousness they had obtained by the direct path of belief. The abundance of preceding sins therefore called for the help of such abundant mercy: unless the forgiver’s generosity had been so great, no other discipline could have helped diseases so serious. But in commending this divine benefit, the apostle saw room for an objection from people who might say: ‘If we rightly assess the worth of causes by their effects, and the abundance of sins obtained an outpouring of God’s mercy, we should persist in sins so that grace’s abundance does not fail.’ Anticipating such an opinion, he says: ‘What, then, shall we say? Shall we remain in sin so that grace may abound? Far from it! For we who died to sin, how shall we still live in it? Or do you not know that all of us baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? We were therefore buried with him through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ rose in the Father’s glory, we too might walk in newness of life’ (Romans 6:1–4).

He says that we died to sin at the time when, to receive the gift of forgiveness, we professed our renunciation of the world and all sins. Remembering the gift, we should therefore live in a way that shows we have been buried with Christ and visibly bear his resurrection in holiness. Just as, after rising from the dead, he undergoes no bodily weakness or scourging, so we too should strive to be invulnerable to all sins and vices. ‘For if we have been planted together in the likeness of his death, we shall also share his resurrection, knowing that our old self was crucified with him so that the body of sin might be destroyed, so that we no longer serve sin. For the one who has died has been justified from sin’ (Romans 6:5–7). He binds believers with clear reasoning. If you wish, he says, to share his resurrection, imitate the power of his death too, so that, dead to vices, you may live in virtue. You will share that happiness if you bear the image of his death by dying to sins. Our old self should be shown nailed to his cross, to destroy the body of sin through the courage of suffering. By ‘body of sin,’ according to his customary usage, Paul means vices, not the substance of flesh. For he continues: ‘So that the body of sin might be destroyed, so that we no longer serve sin. For the one who has died has been justified from sin.’

He was, of course, speaking to living people and telling them that righteousness had been conferred on them through the mysteries. How, then, does he say someone is justified whom he calls dead, unless he is showing beyond ambiguity that here he calls renunciation ‘death’? He adopts the name of death to show that believers should cease from sins as dead people cease from activities.

‘For if we died with Christ, we believe that we shall live with Christ, knowing that Christ, raised from the dead, dies no more; death will no longer rule over him. For the death he died to sin, he died once, but the life he lives, he lives to God. So you too reckon yourselves dead to sin but alive to God in Christ Jesus’ (Romans 6:8–11). Just as Christ, he says, died to sin once—that is, died because of our sins once—and dies no more, but lives in God’s glory, so you too, reckoning yourselves dead to sin, should live and serve virtues alone.

Where here is nature accused? Where are the beginnings of human substance blamed? Where is the movement of the one begetting a child condemned? It is clearer than light that the Teacher of the Gentiles addresses only the will, so that it renounces hidden disgrace (2 Corinthians 4:2) and advances to a better life through corrected actions. But now let our explanation take a shorter course and stop continually interpreting the apostle’s words in these passages. Let us hear him discuss his own meaning. At the end of his argument it will become clear whose doctrine and faith he agrees with. We say, of course, that the apostle spoke of the sin of human will, present in each person who sins. You speak of the sin which, believing Faustus, you think was transmitted through generation and received by everyone without willing it. Let our disputes, then, cease, if you please. To proceed modestly, let us set aside the apostle’s dignity. On that ground alone we could insist that, even if his words agreed with you in every respect, he nevertheless could have intended nothing so disgraceful, given the splendor of his office: the fault would lie in ambiguous expressions, not perverse meanings. Let us grant him only this in the present matter: as a man whose mind was not disordered, he should be believed to have understood his own writings better than you do. ‘Therefore,’ he says, ‘do not let sin reign in your mortal body so that you obey it’ (Romans 6:12). I could already say here that the exhortation proves he is treating sins of will. For if evils were natural, they could be defended on grounds of justice or, at least, lamented out of pity; but in no way could people be admonished to avoid them. Greater than any natural evil, if such an evil could exist, would be the evil of the madness possessing anyone who demanded devotion in avoiding natural things. But the apostle enacted nothing that could justly be criticized. He therefore indicates a sin of will when he insists that it must be avoided.

‘Do not present your members as weapons of injustice to sin, but present yourselves to God as people alive from the dead, and your members as weapons of righteousness to God. For sin does not rule over you: you are not under law but under grace’ (Romans 6:13–14). You should, he says, serve God more faithfully because you do so more freely. Sin ruled over you when punishment for guilt hung over you. But after you received the benefits of God’s grace and breathed freely with the weight of your guilt laid down, a free person’s sense of honor should prompt you to show gratitude to your healer.

But this gave occasion for the same question he had explained above: someone might object that people freed from the law, which threatened wrath, could safely sin under the kindness of God’s grace. He therefore immediately added: ‘What then? Shall we sin because we are not under law but under grace? Far from it! Or do you not know that when you present yourselves as slaves for obedience, you are slaves of the one you obey, whether of sin or of obedience to righteousness?’ (Romans 6:15–16). Do we now believe him about the kind of sin he has been discussing? When you present yourselves, he says, as slaves for obedience, you are slaves of that one, whether of sin or righteousness. Where, then, does the apostle indicate here that sin which is imagined to have flown over the very seed before the time of willing, before the activity of obedience, before the age of knowledge and conscience? Such a thing certainly can be found only in Manichaean books.

The apostle, however—if he can obtain any credibility from people in this age—shows that he calls none slaves of sin except those who are known to have obeyed sin by their own will. By changing that will, they began to serve righteousness. He therefore placed obedience in the middle and attributed to it their effort to obey vices earlier and virtues afterward (compare Romans 6:16–18).

english: ‘But thanks be to God,’ he says, ‘that you were slaves of sin, but obeyed from the heart the pattern of teaching to which you were entrusted. Freed from sin, you have become slaves of righteousness’ (Romans 6:17–18).
A change of obedience made from the heart, he says, freed you from sin and made you cling to holiness.

‘What I say is human, because of the weakness of your flesh. For just as you presented your members to serve impurity and lawlessness for lawlessness, so now present your members to serve righteousness for sanctification’ (Romans 6:19). What a teacher, filled with God’s Spirit! Truly a golden vessel, and a trumpet sounding not broken shrieks but clear notes! He gains authority for his words through the humanity of his exhortation.

To avoid seeming to command anything arduous and inaccessible to a human being, he took an expression from ordinary speech and called it ‘human’: that is, easy to handle, something made gentler by comparing the cases. I do not demand of you, he says, an intensity matching these exalted realities; nor, great as virtue’s riches are, do I establish correspondingly novel commands by which you must obtain them. I impose nothing harsh, prescribe nothing barely bearable. If I commanded such a thing in proportion to righteousness’s splendor, you might complain of the flesh’s weakness and plead that you could not bear constant toil. So now I address you with this moderation: apply to virtues the same effort you previously applied to crimes. Although it insults honorable things to pursue them with merely the same determination spent on disgraceful things, it nevertheless suffices for your present training if you pursue righteousness with at least the intensity with which you pursued lawlessness and impurity.
Let us therefore believe the Teacher of the Gentiles and bear witness to his truthfulness. Truly, as he said, what he commanded is human: that correcting the will should amend the will’s vices.

But just as this is human, the other position, if he had held it, would have been not merely inhuman and savage, but unjust—and not merely unjust, but insane. If he knew sin was inborn, he would be reproaching people of his own age with the faults of an ancient birth, commanding abstention from things he believed innate, and prescribing with threats that I must lay down things I had begun to possess before my soul entered my body and my body entered this world.

Those whom he strove to amend would more rightly admonish him to weigh how much he commanded and recognize that the first step of sound counsel is to observe moderation in commands. Teaching is stripped of authority when fairness does not defend it; it is full of authority when justice’s balance commends it. It is therefore established that the apostle, the churches’ revered teacher, giving an account of his teaching through good judgment, fairness, and humanity, meant nothing about natural sin. Rather, he insisted, as was the case, that we had been slaves of vices only through our will, and that through the same will, if corrected, we can serve righteousness. But since I have been occupied this far in explaining this passage, to show that the Manichaeans can find no defense in the apostle Paul’s words, and since the sequence of his discourse has disclosed the truth he follows throughout the entire body of his statements, let this be the end of the second book. Here, however, we must warn that nothing remains for the advocates of inherited sin except shamelessness. They confessed that they had no defense in reason and claimed all their comfort from the apostolic words we have explained. Now that it is clear these prescribe nothing disgraceful, nothing at odds with holiness and reason, their position has plainly fallen. Reason, together with many scriptural authorities, and the catholics’ reverence for God have overthrown it; and the supposed meaning of this passage no longer protects it (compare Romans 6:17–19).
